Chapter 5. Private Struggles, Public Legacy, and the Question of Slavery.
When we picture George Washington, most of us see the steady leader—the father of his country. But if you look a little closer, you’ll find a man who wrestled with inner contradictions and private doubts, long after he stepped away from the presidency.
Retirement at Mount Vernon wasn’t just peaceful reflection. For Washington, it meant facing uncomfortable truths, especially about slavery. His estate was stunning—a home filled with order and beauty. Yet, beneath that surface, it was still a plantation, running on the labor of enslaved people.
Washington’s relationship with slavery was anything but simple. He’d inherited enslaved workers as a young man, and his wealth and social standing depended on their efforts. For a big part of his life, he just accepted slavery as the way things were.
But as he grew older, and the ideals of the Revolution began to sink in, he started to question the very foundation of that system. The change didn’t happen overnight. There was a lot of hesitation, a fair amount of doubt. He worried about what freeing his enslaved workers might mean—financially, legally, and personally. Would it cause chaos for both him and the people he wanted to help? What would it mean for the future of the country? And what kind of legacy would he actually leave behind?
So many in his position might have simply looked away, avoiding the discomfort. Washington, though cautious, felt the tension between his public principles and his private reality. He couldn’t just ignore it.
In those final years at Mount Vernon, Washington made choices that set him apart from many of his peers. In his will, he arranged for the gradual emancipation of his enslaved workers, making sure they’d be cared for and supported. It wasn’t a sweeping gesture—there were limits, shaped by the world he lived in. But it showed a deepening sense of justice and humanity.
Was it enough to erase the pain or the injustice? No. But it offered a glimpse of a man willing to reflect, to grow, and to try, even late in life, to do better.
Washington’s legacy is a patchwork of great achievements and very real imperfections. He set the bar for integrity and self-restraint, and he understood the power of example. But he was also a product of his times—with all the blind spots that came with it.
If there’s one big takeaway, it’s this—his story isn’t about flawless heroism. It’s about wrestling with hard truths, growing in the face of them, and never giving up on the effort to live up to the ideals he helped shape.
